title: pkix-chain: async verify path (requires an async Verifier, not a wrapper)
description:
## Why

PKIX-j32w.3 decided pkix-chain would grow an async twin of its DANE-relevant verify entry points, and recorded that the async path must be async ALL THE WAY DOWN: an entry point that awaited TLSA resolution and then called a synchronous RevocationChecker or AiaFetcher would block the executor on that I/O, which is the defect already open against pkix-revocation-http as PKIX-cr8.1 and PKIX-f1j4.10.

The sync DANE composition shipped in pkix-chain 0.6.0. The async twin did not, because implementing it revealed the scope is materially larger than "add async siblings to a few functions".

## The actual scope

verify_tls_server does not perform validation itself. It calls verify_chain, which constructs a Verifier and calls verify_one, which calls:

- build_with_aia -- roughly 99 lines, and itself calls try_build
- run_revocation_checks -- roughly 18 lines

Both touch the I/O traits. So an async verify_tls_server_dane needs an async Verifier with async counterparts of verify_one, build_with_aia, try_build and run_revocation_checks, generic over AsyncRevocationChecker and AsyncAiaFetcher instead of their sync forms. That is duplicating pkix-chain's orchestration layer, not wrapping it.

Everything it depends on now exists: AsyncTlsaResolver (pkix-dane-resolver 0.2.0), AsyncRevocationChecker (pkix-revocation-http, behind its async feature), AsyncAiaFetcher (pkix-aia-http 0.3.0, PKIX-j72x). The missing piece is entirely inside pkix-chain.

## Decide before building

1. Duplicate or unify. A parallel AsyncVerifier is straightforward and matches how pkix-revocation-http handled the same problem, but it doubles the orchestration surface -- and build_with_aia is where the AIA bounds from PKIX-zkjb.7 live, so the two copies drifting is a correctness risk, not just a maintenance one. The alternative is making the orchestration generic over a sync-or-async I/O abstraction, which is more invasive and may not be worth it. Decide explicitly rather than defaulting to duplication because it is easier to start.

2. Scope of the async surface. PKIX-j32w.3 recorded that only DANE-relevant entry points need async siblings, and that adding the rest on symmetry grounds buys nothing. That still holds, but verify_one and verify_batch are generic entry points consumers use directly, so decide whether they get async forms too.

3. SignatureVerifier stays sync -- signature verification is CPU-bound, nothing to await. Note that PKIX-cr8.1 and PKIX-f1j4.10 argue ms-scale CPU inside an async fn is itself a problem deserving spawn_blocking. That question is broader than DANE and should not be settled here, but it will come up.

## Acceptance

[ ] Duplicate-or-unify decision recorded before code is written
[ ] An async DANE entry point exists that awaits TLSA resolution, revocation AND AIA -- no sync I/O trait on the async path
[ ] AIA bounds (per-cert URI cap, total fetch cap, deadline) behave identically on both paths, with tests that would fail if the two copies drifted
[ ] The sync path is unchanged
close_reason:
CLOSED 2026-11-24, by reversing the decision that created it rather than implementing it.

## Outcome

pkix-chain gained a PUBLIC sans-I/O verify surface instead of an async twin. 163 tests (was 155); fmt / clippy / rustdoc -D warnings / typos clean.

- pub mod sans_io: ChainBuilder, ChainBuildState, BuildStep for AIA reassembly as a state machine; revocation_targets + RevocationTarget for the revocation checks a validated chain calls for; build_with as a convenience driver for synchronous callers; Verifier::chain_builder.
- pkix-chain gained NO async feature, NO async-trait, NO HTTP dependency.

## Why the async twin was the wrong answer

This bead already recorded the first problem: verify_tls_server performs no validation itself, so an async path that is async all the way down needed an async Verifier duplicating verify_one, build_with_aia, try_build and run_revocation_checks. build_with_aia is where the AIA bounds from PKIX-zkjb.7 live, and two copies of a BOUND drifting is a security regression, not a maintenance annoyance.

A second problem surfaced while scoping it, and this bead had not anticipated it. The async traits live in the std HTTP adapters (AsyncAiaFetcher in pkix-aia-http, AsyncRevocationChecker in pkix-revocation-http), so for pkix-chain to be generic over them it must depend on BOTH HTTP client crates -- ureq and reqwest and transitively tokio -- purely to name two traits. The sync case has the opposite shape: those traits live in the no_std cores and pkix-chain depends only on those. An orchestrator depending on two HTTP clients is backwards, and the three ways out all had real costs: move the async traits into the no_std cores (changes four shipped crates, and revisits the Option C rejection from PKIX-a1yc.10), accept the dependency weight, or add a fifth crate holding two trait definitions.

## What dissolved the question

build_with_aia is ninety-odd lines around ONE network call. Everything else is pure bookkeeping. Extracting that bookkeeping -- done first as a no-behaviour-change refactor, verified by the existing AIA tests passing unchanged -- left a state machine. Making it public means a caller on any runtime drives verification while owning every fetch, and pkix-chain never needs an async trait at all.

The sync path now delegates to the same driver, so there is exactly ONE reassembly loop rather than one per path. run_revocation_checks takes its work from revocation_targets, so the sync path and a caller driving the checks cannot disagree about what needs checking.

This is the same move the DANE epic records for PKIX-apmt: the question dissolves rather than getting answered.

## A design considered and rejected

"The caller pre-fetches everything, then calls sync validation" -- the shape that worked for TLSA records -- does NOT work for AIA. The fetch targets depend on the previous round's results, so a caller cannot know what to fetch in advance without reimplementing the caps, the deduplication and the deadline. Worth recording because it is the obvious first idea.

## Consequence for the async story

An async consumer writes a ten-line loop rather than awaiting one function. The epic's convenience goal, already trimmed twice, is trimmed a third time -- and this is the trim that buys the most: no duplicated orchestration, no inverted dependency, no runtime lock-in, and nothing shipped had to change.

The async traits in pkix-aia-http and pkix-revocation-http are NOT wasted. They remain the right seam for a consumer plugging their own async client into those adapters; what changed is that pkix-chain does not need to be generic over them.

## Acceptance, as filed

[x] Duplicate-or-unify decision recorded before code was written -- answered with a third option, extract-the-pure-core, recorded here and in the commit
[x] An async path exists that awaits TLSA resolution, revocation AND AIA with no sync I/O trait on it -- achieved by the caller owning all three, demonstrated in tests/sans_io.rs from a tokio task
[x] AIA bounds behave identically on both paths -- not by testing two copies but by there being one; tests/sans_io.rs asserts the caps and the once-per-URI rule hold on the sans-I/O path rather than only through the wrapper
[x] The sync path is unchanged -- existing AIA tests pass unchanged, which is what verified the extraction
